title.narrative: The Gambia Second Fiscal Management, Energy and Telecom Reform Development Policy Financing

description.narrative: The development objectives of the Second Fiscal Management, Energy and Telecom Reform Development Policy Financing in Gambia are to: (i) improve debt and public investment management; (ii) improve financial viability and service delivery in the energy and telecom sectors; and (iii) enhance the transparency and governance framework of State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs). It supports the authorities efforts to address critical bottlenecks to sustained inclusive growth and supports three key pillars. Pillar 1, debt and public investment management supports: (i) strengthening fiscal risks and debt management by introducing a framework to manage government loan guarantees and issuing an annual borrowing plan; (ii) strengthening public investment management by improving project selection and appraisal; and (iii) implementing the procurement act to ensure consistent use of competitive bidding and proper oversight of the procurement process. Pillar 2, financial viability and service delivery in the energy and telecom sectors supports strengthening the overall financial position and governance framework of the National Water and Electricity Company through a new tariff compensation mechanism, and the introduction of performance contract and quarterly performance monitoring framework. Pillar 3, transparency and governance framework of SOEs supports: enhancing fiscal transparency, reducing fiscal risks, and improving the corporate government of SOEs through establishing an oversight institution to ensure greater accountability of financial operations.

The program development objective is to (i) improve debt and public investment management; (ii) improve financial viability and service delivery in the energy and telecom sectors; and (iii) enhance the transparency and governance framework of State-owned Enterprises (SOEs).

title.narrative: RI 6: NAWEC aggregated technical, commercial and collection losses (electricity, percent)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The objective of reducing aggregated losses was key to improving service delivery and was partially achieved</strong>. NAWEC aggregated technical, commercial and collection losses dropped to 22 percent in 2023, down from 25 percent in 2019. Although the target of 20 percent in 2022 is not achieved, NAWEC efforts over the period 2019-2023 should be acknowledged. Existing losses are attributed to delays in installing new lines triggered by financial constraints and dispute settlements in courts, and the ongoing replacement of old meters.</p>

title.narrative: RI 8: Proportion of base stations using the ECOWAN with transmission via fiber optic network (percent of total)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The objective of ensuring higher speed and quality of the mobile network through 4G services was not achieved</strong>. Data received from the Public Utility Regulation Authority (PURA) indicate that 49.1 percent of base stations are connected to the ECOWAN network in 2023, compared to 20 percent in 2019. Despite this increase, the actual outcome is below the target of 60 percent in 2022 established in DPF2. The few improvements in connections to the ECOWAN reported by PURA is consistent with the findings of the 2023 report on achievements published by the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy (MOCDE). The latter indicated that 947 km of ECOWAN have been rolled out in the country, against 817 km reported in the Gambia Digital Economy Diagnostic (2021), represening an increase of only 16 percent in four years.</p>

title.narrative: RI 7: Proportion of female directors in NAWEC leadership team (percent of total)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The objective of reducing the gender gap in leadership positions has been achieved since 2021</strong>. Following the introduction of its gender policy, the proportion of female directors in NAWEC increased to 40 percent in 2021, from 10 percent in 2019, and has remained at the same level since then.</p>

title.narrative: RI 3: Share of new projects approved by SRB in a three-year PIP (Percent)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The objective of improving public investment management in The Gambia was not achieved</strong>. The target of 50 percent of new projects approved by the Strategic Review Board (SRB) within the three-year Public Investment Program (PIP) is not achieved because the Government is yet to develop a unified PIP guiding projects approval by the SRB. A pilot study for a unified PIP was doe on five sectors including (Agriculture, Education, Health, Infrastructure and Energy) and list of pipeline projects were submitted by the mentioned sectors for inclusion in the PIP as piloted sectors. The complete roll out to other sectors is expected to be completed at end 2023-second quarter 2024. However, a report from the PFM Directorate for the second half of 2023 indicates that about 90 percent of sectoral ministries, departments and agencies have been trained and now utilize the new project performance appraisal template shared with them by the SRB to review and appraise projects before their approval. Despite this improvement in the appraisal process of projects, the result indicator is assessed as not achieved since the three-year PIP is yet to be developed.</p>

title.narrative: RI 2: Coverage of government loan guarantees in public debt reporting (percent)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The program managed to strengthen debt management and transparency as results indicators 1 and 2 were achieved</strong>. The deviation between domestic debt issuance and the annual borrowing plan is assessed at 21 percent in 2023, lower than the target of 25 percent set for 2022. The Gambia sixth review under the current IMF ECF program (2020-2024) indicates that the ceiling on net domestic borrowing was met with a margin of 0.7 percent of GDP at end-December 2022. Result indicator 2 on the Coverage of governmet loan guarantees in public debt reporting (in percent) is assessed as achieved on the basis that there are no government loan guarantees in public reporting, in 2023 because the last guarantees matured in 2022. There is therefore no need to report loan guarantees in official public debt documents.</p>

title.narrative: RI 10:Transfers and subsidies to SOEs (Percent of GDP)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The objective of reducing the fiscal burden of SOEs was somewhat achieved</strong>. National fiscal data reveals recurrent expenditures on transfers to SOEs represented 0.4 percent of GDP in 2022, lower than the target of 0.5 percent of GDP in 2022 set by the DPF series. This outcome is corroborated by the IMF Article IV Report No. 24/15 from January 2024, which indicates that tota transfers and subsidies by the Government lowered reflecting a stronger commitment from the authorities to fiscal consolidation. The report further mentions that to enhance fiscal sustainability, the authorities will rationalize subsidies to the NFSPC (former Gambia Groundnut Corporation), NAWEC, and subsidized agencies.</p>

title.narrative: RI 5: NAWEC current ratio (current assets /current liabilities)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The objective of improving NAWEC’s financial viability was delayed due to unfavorable oil price developments and delays in addressing revenue mobilization challenges, and the new tariff coming into effect only in April 2023.</strong> The current ratio (current assets/current liabilities) deteriorated to 0.32 in 2022, down from 0.86 in 2019, for two main reasons. From the liability side, hikes in fuel prices in 2022 (heavy fuel and light fuel) significantly impacted NAWEC by generating about US$ 12 milion of additional costs to produce electricity which is 100 percent thermal (i.e., entirely fuel dependent). This unexpected outcome was compounded by the severe forex shortages that the country experienced in the second half of 2022.  From the revenue side, public entities and other SOEs accumulated payments arrears as their financial resources further depleted as the country faced unexpected challenges. Moreover, the implementation of the yearly tariff review process by NAWEC to ensure that the company always has the required revenue for its operations, experienced significant delays. The process was only concluded in February 2023 and the new tariff came into effect in April 2023, helping stabilize the downward trend in revenues</p>

title.narrative: RI 11: Timely publication of annual audited financial statements for all SOEs (years)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The objective of improving the transparency of SOEs was not achieved</strong>. Result indicator 11 on the timely publication of annual (independent) audited financial statements for all SOEs from 2 years in 2019 to within a year by 2022, is unmet. The Gambia latest Article IV report under the current IMF program indicates significant backlogs of external audited financial statements for 2022 and 2023. The latest SOEs Operational and Financial report from MOFEA (2022) indicates that only 2021 audited financial statements are uploaded on the MOFEA website, implying that the said statements are still published once every two years, despite the support of the DPF series. The authorities continue to face challenges, including (i) high fees of the few external auditors in the country who prioritize contracts with commercial banks as the only entities able to afford such expensive services; and (ii) the lak of a sanction mechanism as the one put in place by the Central Bank in monitoring commercial banks’ activities. Nevertheless, such mechanisms are reported to be rolled out progressively and should be effective by the end of 2024 as the Government continues signing performance contracts with SOEs.</p>

title.narrative: RI 9: Share of urban population covered by 4G network (percent of total)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Liberalizing the international gateways allowed a significant increase in the share of population covered by 4G</strong>. Data from PURA indicated that 94 percent of urban population and 46 percent of rural population was covered by the 4G network in 2023, bringing the countrywide population coverage to 72 percent. This result indicator was changed after DPF1 to reflect the breakdown between rural and urban population with baselines of 3 percent and 33 percent, respectively, in 2019. With the support of the operation, the shares of rural and urban population covered by the 4G network was expected to increase to 10 percent and 60 percent, respectively. While results on this indicator appear to be highly satisfactory, it is worth highlighting they are sensitive to the method of calculation. Indeed, we have received conflicting figures from the MOCDE and PURA on the same indicator.</p>

title.narrative: RI 4: Value of single source contracting regulated by the GPPA (percent of total)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>1.            </strong><strong>The efficiency of public procurement seems to have improved, but the objective is assessed as only partially achieved since non-competitive procurement practices continue to be widespread.</strong> Since the passage of the procurement act in October 2022, after the DPF timeline, single source procedures for public procurement can only be used under exceptional circumstances of extreme urgency or specific technical reasons to be justified, irrespective of the estimated value of the contract. Since then, The Gambia Public Procurement Authority reported not having exceeded by too much the threshold of 30 percent of contracts (on value basis) under its jurisdiction that were procured through single source contracting. The share of single source represented 35 percent of the total value of contracts submitted to GPPA in 2023. However, because the Procurement Act, as passed in end-2022, did not eliminate many exemptions and waivers, RI #4 is less relvant to measuring PDO achievement.  As of 2023, the PFM directorate of MOFEA reported that following the passage of the new procurement act, eight public institutions (including underperforming SOEs such as GAMTEL and GAMCEL) have been authorized to proceed with all their procurement without seeking prior approval from GPPA. As a result, the outcome of 35 percent of procurement contracts passed via single source contracting may not fully reflect improvements in reducing noncompetitive procurement practices and conflit of interest.  For that reason, the result indicator is assessed as partially achieved.</p>
